opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because "overfitting" has such a negative connotation in the classic machine learning sense. When we train a general-purpose model, the goal is to generalize as broadly as possible: answer any question, write any kind of code, handle any domain. That's incredibly powerful, but it's also expensive, and most real-world applications don't actually need all of that breadth.

When a company builds a product, they have a very specific job to be done. It might be customer support for their particular product line, or code completion in their codebase, or extracting fields from a certain type of document. In that context, you don't care whether the model can write poetry or explain quantum physics. You care that it's extremely good, extremely fast, and extremely cheap at that one task. So deliberately "overfitting" to that application, by tuning the model on their data, their workflows, and their quality bar, is exactly what you want.

What we've seen is that when you specialize like that, you can often take a much smaller model and get quality that matches or even beats a frontier general model on that narrow task. And because the model is smaller, latency drops dramatically and cost goes way down, which matters a lot once you're serving millions of requests. It also gives the developer more control. They own that customization, it reflects their proprietary data, and that becomes part of their competitive moat rather than everyone using the same off-the-shelf model.

So I'd reframe it a bit: it's not overfitting in the bad sense of memorizing noise. It's specialization. You're aligning the model tightly to the distribution of inputs your application actually sees. For production AI, that alignment between the model and the use case is where a lot of the real value gets unlocked.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think the word "overfitting" carries a lot of baggage from the research world, where it's almost always a bad thing. But when you move into production, the goals shift quite a bit.

In research, you're chasing generality. You want a model that performs well across many benchmarks, many domains, because that's how you demonstrate progress. But when you're a company building a product, you don't actually care about the general case. You care about your case. You have a specific set of users, a specific distribution of queries, a specific set of constraints around latency and cost. A model that's a little worse on everything else but a lot better on your workload is, in practical terms, a better model for you.

So what I mean by "overfitting" in this context is really about specialization. You take a strong general model and you push it toward your application through fine-tuning, through distillation, through tuning on your own production traffic. And the trade-off you're making is that you give up some of that broad capability in exchange for quality, speed, and cost efficiency on the narrow set of things that actually matter to your product.

And there's a second piece to this, which is that smaller, specialized models are just much easier to serve. If you can get a model that's a fraction of the size and matches or beats the big general model on your task, your inference costs drop dramatically, your latency drops, and you can iterate much faster. For a lot of real applications, that's the difference between something being economically viable and not.

So I'd say the instinct against overfitting is right in the lab, but in production, deliberately narrowing the model to your application is often exactly what you should be doing.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by overfitting. If you mean memorizing your training data and then failing on new examples, that’s still a problem. But if you mean specializing a model for a particular application, that can be very desirable. You don’t necessarily need a model that does everything well. You need one that does your task really well.

When the application has a well-defined scope, you can optimize for its data, its requirements, and the kinds of errors that matter most. You may give up some generality, but gain accuracy and efficiency. The important thing is to test on unseen examples that reflect real usage, so you know that specialization actually helps.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, when we talk about overfitting, we usually mean fitting the training data so closely that the model doesn’t generalize to new examples. That’s still something you want to avoid. But specializing a model for a particular application can be very desirable, because you don’t necessarily need it to do everything. You need it to do that application’s job really well.

If you understand the workload, you can optimize the model around the quality, latency, and cost requirements that matter for that use case. You may give up some generality, but that can be a good tradeoff. The key is that it should still generalize to the new inputs it will encounter within that application.
